lines: Objective: quantify impact of 3-DC vs 5-DC configuration on total cost-to-serve (CTS).
Current state: 5 DCs (Reno, Tulsa, Harrisburg, Macon, Ontario). Annual vol = 3.4M orders.
Alt Option A: consolidate to 3 regional hubs (Reno, Columbus, Atlanta).
BUT linehaul miles increase by +11% (avg 612 → 681 mi per shipment).
Last-mile drivers: residential surcharge up 8.5%, rural density factor biggest driver in Dakotas + MT.
Parcel zone shift under 3-DC model: 38% orders move from Zone 4 to Zone 6+.
Estimated parcel cost increase = +$3.9M (higher zones + DAS fees).
Inventory holding reduction from pooling effect ≈ -$2.2M (safety stock ↓ 14%).
Service level risk: 2-day coverage drops from 92% → 84% unless air expedite added.
If add selective air (top 12 SKUs, 9% volume) cost +$1.6M, restores 2-day to 90%.
Action: request carrier rebid on Midwest lanes + evaluate micro-fulfillment in Upper Plains.

spec.title: Network Cost-to-Serve Assessment – Distribution Centre Footprint Scenarios
spec.subtitle: Ref: NCO-27-26 | Date: 18 February 2026 | From: Supply Chain Analytics | To: VP Logistics

sections.heading: Executive Overview
sections.body: This page summarises the quantitative comparison of three alternative distribution-centre (DC) configurations and their impact on total cost-to-serve across the UK and Ireland network. The current four-DC footprint (Leeds, Bristol, Luton, and Glasgow) was benchmarked against a consolidated three-DC model and an expanded five-DC regionalised model. The analysis integrates linehaul rates, carrier lane performance, inventory carrying cost, and last-mile delivery drivers. Results indicate that targeted footprint consolidation combined with lane reallocation can reduce annualised cost-to-serve by 8.4% while maintaining 96% next-day service coverage.

sections.heading: Distribution Centre Configuration Comparison
sections.body: Under the three-DC scenario (Leeds, Luton, and a new Midlands facility in Rugby), average outbound miles per order increased by 6% but linehaul consolidation reduced trunking cost by £2.3M annually. The five-DC model reduced last-mile distance by 11% but added £3.1M in fixed facility and labour overhead. Inventory duplication in the five-DC option increased working capital by £4.7M due to higher safety stock requirements. The three-DC configuration achieved the optimal balance between fixed overhead and transport variable cost.

sections.heading: Carrier Lane Performance Analysis
sections.body: Lane-level performance data from January–December 2025 shows significant cost variance between primary and secondary carriers on the North-West and South Coast corridors. The Manchester–Southampton lane averaged £1.82 per mile with Carrier A versus £2.09 per mile with Carrier C, despite comparable on-time performance (97.1% vs 96.4%). Reallocating 40% of underperforming secondary carrier volume to higher-efficiency partners would yield approximately £780K in annual savings. Service reliability remains within the contractual 95% OTIF threshold under the proposed reallocation.

sections.heading: Last-Mile Cost Drivers
sections.body: Last-mile delivery accounts for 52% of total cost-to-serve, with parcel density, fuel surcharge variability, and failed delivery attempts as the primary drivers. Rural Welsh and Highland Scottish postcodes exhibit delivery costs 34% above network average due to low drop density and extended route times. Introducing micro-consolidation points in Swansea and Inverness reduces redelivery attempts by an estimated 18%. Additionally, tightening delivery window selection for B2C orders could lower accessorial charges by approximately £420K per annum.

sections.heading: Recommended Network Adjustments
sections.body: We recommend adopting the three-DC configuration centred on Leeds, Rugby, and Luton, coupled with structured lane reassignment and targeted last-mile interventions. This redesign is projected to reduce total annual logistics spend from £64.5M to £59.1M without degrading next-day coverage below 95%. Implementation would require phased inventory rebalancing over two quarters and renegotiation of five carrier lane contracts. Risk assessment indicates moderate transition complexity but high recurring financial benefit.

structure.full_text:
Network Cost-to-Serve Assessment – Distribution Centre Footprint Scenarios
Ref: NCO-27-26 | Date: 18 February 2026 | From: Supply Chain Analytics | To: VP Logistics

Section Executive Overview
This page summarises the quantitative comparison of three alternative distribution-centre (DC) configurations and their impact on total cost-to-serve across the UK and Ireland network. The current four-DC footprint (Leeds, Bristol, Luton, and Glasgow) was benchmarked against a consolidated three-DC model and an expanded five-DC regionalised model. The analysis integrates linehaul rates, carrier lane performance, inventory carrying cost, and last-mile delivery drivers. Results indicate that targeted footprint consolidation combined with lane reallocation can reduce annualised cost-to-serve by 8.4% while maintaining 96% next-day service coverage.

Section Distribution Centre Configuration Comparison
Under the three-DC scenario (Leeds, Luton, and a new Midlands facility in Rugby), average outbound miles per order increased by 6% but linehaul consolidation reduced trunking cost by £2.3M annually. The five-DC model reduced last-mile distance by 11% but added £3.1M in fixed facility and labour overhead. Inventory duplication in the five-DC option increased working capital by £4.7M due to higher safety stock requirements. The three-DC configuration achieved the optimal balance between fixed overhead and transport variable cost.

Section Carrier Lane Performance Analysis
Lane-level performance data from January–December 2025 shows significant cost variance between primary and secondary carriers on the North-West and South Coast corridors. The Manchester–Southampton lane averaged £1.82 per mile with Carrier A versus £2.09 per mile with Carrier C, despite comparable on-time performance (97.1% vs 96.4%). Reallocating 40% of underperforming secondary carrier volume to higher-efficiency partners would yield approximately £780K in annual savings. Service reliability remains within the contractual 95% OTIF threshold under the proposed reallocation.

Section Last-Mile Cost Drivers
Last-mile delivery accounts for 52% of total cost-to-serve, with parcel density, fuel surcharge variability, and failed delivery attempts as the primary drivers. Rural Welsh and Highland Scottish postcodes exhibit delivery costs 34% above network average due to low drop density and extended route times. Introducing micro-consolidation points in Swansea and Inverness reduces redelivery attempts by an estimated 18%. Additionally, tightening delivery window selection for B2C orders could lower accessorial charges by approximately £420K per annum.

Section Recommended Network Adjustments
We recommend adopting the three-DC configuration centred on Leeds, Rugby, and Luton, coupled with structured lane reassignment and targeted last-mile interventions. This redesign is projected to reduce total annual logistics spend from £64.5M to £59.1M without degrading next-day coverage below 95%. Implementation would require phased inventory rebalancing over two quarters and renegotiation of five carrier lane contracts. Risk assessment indicates moderate transition complexity but high recurring financial benefit.
